newsitem.title: USA: SEC approves option models for capital regulation.
newsitem.headline: SEC approves option models for capital regulation.

text.p: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) chairman Arthur Levitt said the commission has approved the use of option pricing models for capital requirement rules for broker-dealers.

"This approach had favorable results and I am pleased to announce today that the commission has just approved permanent amendments to the net capital rule that codify the use of option pricing models," Levitt said in a speech to a Risk Management Conference here.

Since 1994, the SEC had permitted broker-dealers to use theoretical option pricing models to calculate required net capital for listed options and related positions that hedged those positions, Levitt said.
"I expect that these amendments will reflect the risk inherent in broker-dealer options positions more accurately," he added.
"Their approval marks the first time the commission has formally adopted and permitted the use of modeling techniques for regulatory capital purposes," he said.

He noted that the measure reflected the SEC's response to the derivatives industry's concerns about costs of regulations. He also said that the SEC was also considering the so-called value-at-risk model for capital regulation.

"The objective of the value-at-risk model is to determine how changes in market conditions may affect the value of a portfolio over a given period of time with a given level of probability," he explained.
"I want to make it clear today that, while we're willing to consider this and other ideas, more work needs to be done," he said.
Levitt further added that the SEC was considering creating a new class of broker-dealer registration for firms' derivatives subsidiaries.
"This new class of limited-purpose broker-dealers would be subject to special regulatory requirements tailored to the derivatives business," he said.
"Not only would this facilitate derivatives transactions, it would also improve our oversight of the derivatives market," he said.
He said the SEC was trying to introduce regulations that are "less burdensome but not less effective."

Levitt stressed that he was an advocate of self-regulation but warned that whenever a fresh financial scandal involving derivatives trading surfaced, he had had to face calls from Washington lawmakers for a "knee-jerk regulation."
Levitt also voiced his concerns about brokers paying so-called "soft dollars" to money managers who bring in business -- a practice some call "frequent flyer miles of the brokerage business."

"I well understand that the law allows soft dollar payments under certain circumstances," he said. "To my mind, however, there are some hard questions that need to be answered. Doesn't the practice threaten to erode investor confidence?"

"I would take special care to ensure that the services provided or obtained are of benefit to the client, not merely the managers," Levitt said. "It would be far better for you to catch and correct any violations than to leave it to the SEC."
